71.sec: DDUGJY - feeder separation, village electrification milestone

71.s: The village electrification milestone achieved under DDUGJY was described by the IEA as:
o: The largest urban distribution reform in India
One of the world's greatest success stories
The first nuclear electrification project in Asia
71.x: The International Energy Agency described the electrification of all inhabited census villages as one of the world's greatest success stories.
71.tq: Identify the distinctive external assessment associated with the milestone.
71.sec: DDUGJY - feeder separation, village electrification milestone

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS):
1. It was approved in 2021.
2. Its approved outlay was ₹3,03,758 crore.
3. Its Gross Budgetary Support was ₹97,631 crore.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: RDSS was approved in 2021 with an outlay of ₹3,03,758 crore, including Gross Budgetary Support of ₹97,631 crore.
71.tq: Test the year, total outlay and budgetary-support figure together.
71.sec: RDSS - smart meters, loss-reduction targets, outlay

71.s: The national targets of RDSS include:
o: AT&C losses of 12–15% and an ACS-ARR gap of zero
AT&C losses of zero and an ACS-ARR gap of 12–15%
AT&C losses of 30% and an ACS-ARR gap of 15%
Only reduction of transmission losses, without an ACS-ARR target
71.x: RDSS aims at pan-India AT&C losses of 12–15% and an ACS-ARR gap of zero.
71.tq: Avoid reversing the two performance indicators and their target values.
71.sec: RDSS - smart meters, loss-reduction targets, outlay

71.s: Which of the following is a principal intervention under RDSS?
o: Prepaid smart metering and loss-reduction works
Replacement of all agricultural feeders by rooftop solar
Free LPG refills and improved stove design
71.x: RDSS focuses on prepaid smart metering and works for reducing distribution losses.
71.tq: Match the operational intervention with the distribution-sector reform scheme.
71.sec: RDSS - smart meters, loss-reduction targets, outlay

71.s: Which component of PM-KUSUM relates to decentralised grid-connected solar or renewable-energy plants on farm or barren land?
71.x: Component A provides for decentralised grid-connected solar or renewable-energy plants on farm or barren land.
71.tq: Match the component letter with its specific intervention.

71.s: Under PM-KUSUM, Component B and Component C respectively refer to:
o: Solarisation of grid-connected pumps; standalone solar pumps
Urban rooftop solar; prepaid smart meters
Standalone solar pumps; solarisation of grid-connected pumps
Farm solar plants; rural feeder separation
71.x: Component B covers standalone solar pumps, while Component C covers solarisation of grid-connected pumps.
71.tq: Discriminate between the two closely related pump components.
71.sec: PM-KUSUM - components A, B, C; subsidy sharing

71.s: PM-KUSUM was launched in 2019 by which ministry?
o: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy

71.tq: Use the ministry and launch year to separate PM-KUSUM from other rural schemes.

71.tq: Check the three-way percentage split without confusing it with rooftop-solar CFA.
71.sec: PM-KUSUM - components A, B, C; subsidy sharing

71.s: Decentralised solarisation under PM-KUSUM provides daytime irrigation and additional income to approximately how many farmers?
71.x: Decentralised solarisation provides daytime irrigation and extra income to over 21.77 lakh farmers.
71.tq: Distinguish the farmer-beneficiary count from the pump-installation counts.
71.sec: PM-KUSUM - components A, B, C; subsidy sharing

71.s: The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana was launched in 2016 by the:
o: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
71.x: PMUY was launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to provide deposit-free LPG connections to poor women.
71.tq: Match the clean-cooking scheme with its administrative ministry.

71.s: What was the Phase I target of PMUY by 2019?
71.x: Phase I of PMUY targeted 8 crore deposit-free LPG connections by 2019; the reported number of connections later exceeded 9.5 crore.
71.tq: Distinguish the original target from the later cumulative achievement.
71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: Which of the following is correctly associated with Ujjwala 2.0?
o: Free first refill and stove, self-declaration facility for migrants, and ₹1,600 assistance per 14.2 kg connection
Free electricity up to 300 units and 60% rooftop-solar subsidy
A ₹6,521 crore package for border villages only
71.x: Ujjwala 2.0 provides a free first refill and stove, permits migrants to use self-declaration, and provides cash assistance of ₹1,600 per 14.2 kg connection.
71.tq: Group several features belonging to one phase instead of mixing schemes.
71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: Since October 2023, the targeted subsidy for PMUY beneficiaries has been:
o: ₹200 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 12 refills a year
₹300 per 5 kg refill without an annual limit
₹1,600 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 5 refills a year
₹300 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 9 refills a year
71.x: Since October 2023, the targeted subsidy has been ₹300 per 14.2 kg refill for up to nine refills a year. Older provisions cited ₹200 and up to 12 refills.
71.tq: Give priority to the latest figure while distinguishing it from the older subsidy arrangement.
71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: Which of the following best explains the refill issue faced by many PMUY households?
o: They are prohibited from obtaining LPG refills after the first connection.
They want clean fuel but face cost and habit-related barriers.
They lack any interest in clean fuel and reject LPG completely.
They are supplied only with solar cooking devices.
71.x: Survey findings indicate that households generally want clean fuel but face affordability and established-habit barriers to regular refilling.
71.tq: Select the option that captures both demand for clean fuel and the practical constraint.
71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Surya Nutan — launched by REC as a rural feeder programme
Grameen Vitrak Yojana — raised the rural share of LPG distributors from 18% to 60%
Grameen Vitrak Yojana — introduced prepaid smart meters under RDSS

71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: Surya Nutan, related to clean cooking access, is:
o: A feeder-separation project launched by the Ministry of Power
An indoor solar stove developed by IOCL in 2022
A rural LPG distribution programme launched in 2009
A rooftop-solar subsidy scheme launched by MNRE in 2024
71.x: Surya Nutan is an indoor solar stove developed by Indian Oil Corporation Limited in 2022.
71.tq: Use the device, developer and year together to identify the initiative.
71.sec: Clean cooking access - PM Ujjwala Yojana, refill issues

71.s: The Integrated Power Development Scheme (IPDS), launched in December 2014, primarily aims to strengthen:
o: Rural agricultural feeder separation and village electrification
Urban sub-transmission and distribution, metering and IT enablement
71.x: IPDS strengthens urban sub-transmission and distribution, metering and IT enablement.
71.tq: Distinguish the urban distribution focus of IPDS from the rural focus of DDUGJY.

71.x: The Integrated Power Development Scheme subsumed the Restructured Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (R-APDRP).

71.s: Which outcome has been credited to IPDS?
o: Universal LPG refilling among rural households
Electrification of all inhabited census villages
71.x: IPDS has been credited with improving urban power supply through strengthening urban distribution infrastructure and metering.
71.tq: Match the reported outcome with the scheme’s urban infrastructure function.
71.sec: IPDS - urban distribution strengthening

71.s: In Andhra Pradesh, free power up to how many units per month is provided to BPL SC/ST households?

71.x: The provision covers 20.26 lakh BPL SC/ST households.
71.tq: Distinguish the precise coverage figure from similar-looking numerical distractors.
71.sec: AP implementation - free power, PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM

71.sec: AP implementation - free power, PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM

71.s: The power subsidy provided in Andhra Pradesh during FY 2024–25 was approximately:

71.s: Free rooftop solar power for SC/ST households in Andhra Pradesh is proposed through:

The Chairperson of the Central Electricity Authority

Household connections → quality and discom viability → prosumers
Household connections → prosumers → quality and discom viability
71.x: The emphasis moved from providing connections through DDUGJY and Saubhagya, to quality and discom viability through UDAY and RDSS, and subsequently to prosumers through PM Surya Ghar.
71.tq: Arrange the policy stages from basic access to system viability and then consumer participation.
71.sec: Universal angles

71.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the principal policy emphasis?
o: UDAY and RDSS — promotion of rooftop prosumers only
PM Surya Ghar — rural electrification connections only
DDUGJY and Saubhagya — electricity connections and access
71.x: DDUGJY and Saubhagya were associated with expanding electricity access and connections. UDAY and RDSS concern quality and discom viability, while PM Surya Ghar promotes prosumer participation.
71.tq: Compare each programme with its dominant policy objective and reject reversed associations.
71.sec: Universal angles

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the current electricity-sector position:
1. India's installed capacity was 509.74 GW.
2. Renewable energy accounted for 49.83 per cent of installed capacity.
3. These figures relate to November 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: All three statements are correct: installed capacity was 509.74 GW and renewable energy constituted 49.83 per cent in November 2025.
71.tq: Link the quantitative values with the correct reference date instead of considering them in isolation.
71.sec: Universal angles

71.s: Which of the following is identified as a continuing criticism of electricity distribution and rooftop-solar expansion?
o: Absence of renewable-energy potential and surplus loan availability
Weak discom finances, slow rooftop uptake and difficulties in accessing loans
Universal adoption of rooftop solar without financing constraints
Complete financial strength of all discoms and excessive rooftop adoption
71.x: The continuing concerns are weak discom finances, slow uptake of rooftop solar and difficulties in accessing loans.
71.tq: Select the option that combines all the stated challenges without reversing their direction.
71.sec: Universal angles

71.s: Which village in Manipur was identified as the last village to be electrified?
71.x: Leisang in Manipur was identified as the last village to be electrified.
71.tq: Use the distinctive place-name association to distinguish the first/last fact from nearby locations.
71.sec: Universal angles

71.s: Leisang, identified as the last village to be electrified, achieved this status on:
71.x: Leisang was electrified on 28 April 2018.
71.tq: Test the exact date using closely spaced annual distractors.
71.sec: Universal angles

73.s: In an ecosystem, the primary source of energy is
73.x: The Sun is the primary energy source for ecosystems. Producers capture solar energy through photosynthesis and transfer it to consumers.
73.tq: Use the direct source-identification approach and distinguish energy input from nutrient cycling.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the direction of energy flow in an ecosystem?
73.x: Energy flows unidirectionally from the Sun to producers and then to consumers. Unlike nutrients, energy is not cycled within the ecosystem.
73.tq: Follow the sequence from the energy source to successive trophic levels.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding energy flow in an ecosystem:
1. Energy flow is unidirectional.
2. Energy is cycled in an ecosystem in the same manner as nutrients.
3. Energy flow obeys the laws of thermodynamics.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Energy flows in one direction and obeys the laws of thermodynamics. Statement 2 is false because nutrients are cycled, whereas energy is not.
73.tq: Find the incorrect statement by separating energy flow from nutrient cycling.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
With reference to incident sunlight and photosynthesis, which of the following statements is correct?
1. Less than 50% of incident sunlight is photosynthetically active radiation.
2. Plants fix approximately 2–10% of photosynthetically active radiation.
3. Plants capture all incident sunlight for photosynthesis.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Less than 50% of incident sunlight is photosynthetically active radiation, and plants fix only about 2–10% of that PAR. Statement 3 is false because plants do not capture all incident sunlight.
73.tq: Reject the extreme statement containing 'all' and retain the two quantified facts.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Primary production efficiency of an ecosystem measures
o: the proportion of solar energy captured and used in photosynthesis
the rate at which consumers form new organic matter
the total energy available at the highest trophic level
the proportion of energy lost through respiration
73.x: Primary production efficiency indicates how much incoming solar energy is captured and used in photosynthesis. Its average value is only about 1–2%.
73.tq: Match the efficiency term with the process it measures rather than with an energy-loss process.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: The average primary production efficiency in an ecosystem is approximately
73.x: On average, only about 1–2% of incoming solar energy is captured and used in photosynthesis as primary production efficiency.
73.tq: Distinguish the average efficiency figure from the broader PAR-fixation range.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes gross primary productivity from net primary productivity?
o: GPP is total organic matter formed by photosynthesis, whereas NPP is GPP minus producer respiration.
GPP is consumer production, whereas NPP is producer production.
GPP is GPP minus respiration, whereas NPP is total photosynthetic production.
GPP and NPP are identical terms for secondary productivity.
73.x: Gross primary productivity is the total rate at which producers form organic matter through photosynthesis. Net primary productivity equals GPP minus the respiration losses of producers.
73.tq: Split the options by checking which term includes respiration losses.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Net primary productivity is important to consumers because it represents
o: the energy remaining after producer respiration and available to herbivores
the energy lost as heat during respiration
the total solar radiation reaching producers
the organic matter formed by consumers alone
73.x: NPP is the gross primary productivity minus producer respiration. It is the energy or organic matter available to herbivores and other consumers.
73.tq: Apply the GPP–NPP relationship to identify the energy actually available to herbivores.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I
(a) Gross primary productivity
(b) Net primary productivity
(c) Secondary productivity

List-II
(i) New organic matter formed by consumers
(ii) Total organic matter made through photosynthesis
(iii) GPP minus producer respiration

Code:
73.x: GPP is the total organic matter produced through photosynthesis; NPP is GPP minus producer respiration; secondary productivity is new organic matter formed by consumers.
73.tq: Start from the sure pair linking secondary productivity with consumers.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: The term ‘secondary productivity’ refers to the rate at which
o: solar radiation is converted into PAR
73.x: Secondary productivity is the rate at which consumers form new organic matter. Primary productivity is associated with producers.
73.tq: Use the producer–consumer distinction to identify the correct productivity term.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Raymond Lindeman’s ten per cent law of energy transfer was formulated in
73.x: Raymond Lindeman formulated the ten per cent law in 1942. The law states that only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
73.tq: Use the year-based numerical distinction among closely spaced values.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: According to the ten per cent law, approximately what proportion of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
73.x: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next level. The remaining approximately 90% is lost through respiration, excretion, locomotion and heat.
73.tq: Separate the transferred fraction from the much larger fraction lost at each trophic transfer.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Assertion (A): Food chains generally do not extend beyond four or five trophic levels.
Reason (R): About 90% of energy is lost at each trophic transfer through processes such as respiration, excretion, locomotion and heat.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
73.x: Both statements are true, and the large energy loss at each transfer leaves insufficient energy to support many successive trophic levels. This explains why food chains are generally limited to four or five levels.
73.tq: Test whether the energy-loss statement directly explains the limited length of food chains.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the energy transformations described by the first and second laws of thermodynamics in an ecosystem?
o: Energy is created at each trophic level and completely retained as biomass
Energy is transformed, while every transfer involves some loss as heat
Energy is destroyed before it reaches producers and regenerated by consumers
Energy remains unchanged and is continuously cycled between trophic levels
73.x: The first law indicates that energy is transformed rather than created or destroyed. The second law indicates that every transfer involves energy loss as heat.
73.tq: Use the paired-law distinction: transformation under the first law and heat loss under the second.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Arrange the following ecosystems in descending order of net primary productivity per unit area:
A. Open ocean
B. Tropical rainforest
C. Desert
D. Estuary

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Tropical rainforests are the most productive among the listed ecosystems, followed by estuaries; open oceans and deserts are among the least productive per unit area, with deserts lower in this comparison.
73.tq: Apply ranking by productivity per unit area and place the two high-productivity systems first.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following ecosystems is generally the most productive in terms of net primary productivity per unit area?
73.x: Tropical rainforests are the standard highest-productivity ecosystem among the alternatives. Estuaries, coral reefs and swamps also have high productivity.
73.tq: Identify the standard high-yield answer while distinguishing productivity per unit area from total output.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following statements about oceanic productivity:
1. Open oceans have low net primary productivity per unit area.
2. The total output of oceans can still be large because of their extensive area.
3. Oceans are necessarily the most productive ecosystems when productivity is measured per unit area.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Open oceans have low productivity per unit area, but their enormous area gives them a large total output. Statement 3 is false because tropical rainforests and certain aquatic ecosystems are more productive per unit area.
73.tq: Watch the reversed comparison between total productivity and productivity per unit area.
73.sec: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding food chains:
1. A grazing food chain begins with living green plants.
2. A detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter.
3. In a grazing food chain, energy captured by autotrophs is transferred to herbivores.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. Grazing chains begin with living producers, whereas detritus chains begin with dead leaves, remains or other dead organic matter.
73.tq: Test the defining starting point and energy-transfer direction of each food-chain type.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: A food chain beginning with leaf litter and proceeding through earthworms to birds is classified as a:
73.x: A detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter such as leaf litter and proceeds through detritivores such as earthworms to higher consumers.
73.tq: Distinguish the two chains by asking whether the first component is living vegetation or dead organic matter.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: In the sequence ‘tiger, grass, snake, frog’, which trophic level is missing?
73.x: Grass represents the first trophic level and the remaining animals are consumers. The second trophic level, occupied by herbivores or primary consumers, is absent.
73.tq: Locate the producer first and identify the absent feeding group between producer and carnivore.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence in an aquatic food chain?
o: Zooplankton → phytoplankton → large fish → small fish
Large fish → small fish → zooplankton → phytoplankton
Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish
Small fish → phytoplankton → zooplankton → large fish
73.x: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are primary consumers, and small and large fish occupy progressively higher trophic positions.
73.tq: Arrange the organisms from producer to successively larger consumers.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s:
Which of the following organisms occupies the first trophic level in an ecosystem?
1. Phytoplankton
2. Seaweeds
3. Green plants
4. Zooplankton
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Phytoplankton, seaweeds and green plants are producers and occupy the first trophic level. Zooplankton are primary consumers at the second trophic level.
73.tq: Separate producers from primary consumers before selecting the coded combination.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Chemosynthetic bacteria found at hydrothermal vents are placed at the first trophic level because they:
o: Obtain chemical energy to manufacture food
Consume small fish and other carnivores
73.x: Chemosynthetic bacteria are producers because they manufacture food using chemical energy rather than sunlight.
73.tq: Apply the definition of a producer to an unusual non-green organism.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Zooplankton — Second trophic level
2. Carnivores — Third or fourth trophic level
3. Phytoplankton — Primary consumers
4. Seaweeds — Producers
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
73.x: Zooplankton are primary consumers at the second trophic level, while carnivores occupy higher levels and seaweeds are producers. Phytoplankton are producers, not primary consumers.
73.tq: Check each organism against its feeding role rather than its habitat.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: With reference to trophic levels, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: A trophic level denotes the functional position of an organism in a food chain.
Each species can occupy only one trophic level in every ecosystem.
A trophic level denotes the geographical location of an organism.
Decomposers always occupy the highest trophic level.
73.x: A trophic level is the functional position occupied by an organism in a food chain. A species may occupy more than one trophic level in different feeding relationships.
73.tq: Choose the precise definition and reject statements using absolute terms such as ‘only’ and ‘always’.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of a food web?
o: It excludes decomposers from energy relationships.
It begins exclusively with dead organic matter.
It contains only one pathway of energy transfer.
It represents interlinked food chains and provides alternative food sources.
73.x: A food web consists of interconnected food chains. It provides species with alternative food sources and generally improves the chances of survival.
73.tq: Identify the defining feature of a web—multiple interconnected feeding pathways.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s:
Assertion (A): Removal of one link in a food web can affect several branches of the web.
Reason (R): A food web consists of interlinked food chains with interconnected energy pathways.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
73.x: Both statements are true, and the interconnected nature of food chains explains why removal of one link can affect subsequent branches.
73.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the ecological consequence stated in the assertion.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Why do food chains rarely extend beyond four or five trophic levels?
o: Producers disappear after the third level.
Too little energy remains available at higher trophic levels.
Decomposers prevent the formation of additional levels.
Carnivores cannot occupy more than one level.
73.x: Energy available to organisms decreases at successive trophic levels. Consequently, insufficient energy remains to support many higher levels.
73.tq: Link the length of a food chain with the progressive reduction of available energy.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism)
 a. Phytoplankton
 b. Zooplankton
 c. Carnivores
 d. Earthworms

List-II (Role)
 i. Primary consumers
 ii. Producers
 iii. Detritivores
 iv. Secondary or tertiary consumers

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are primary consumers, carnivores occupy higher consumer levels, and earthworms are detritivores.
73.tq: Start with the sure producer pair and then match the feeding roles of consumers and detritivores.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Detritus food chain — Begins with dead organic matter
Food web — Single, unconnected feeding pathway
Trophic level — Functional position in a food chain
Grazing food chain — Begins with living green plants
73.x: A food web is made up of interlinked food chains and therefore contains multiple connected feeding pathways, not a single unconnected pathway.
73.tq: Find the option that reverses the defining meaning of the ecological term.
73.sec: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following combinations consists entirely of abiotic components of an ecosystem?
o: Green plants, water, fungi and soil
73.x: Temperature, water, gases and soil are non-living or abiotic components. The other combinations include living organisms.
73.tq: Separate non-living environmental factors from organisms before evaluating the combination.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Radiation is an abiotic component of an ecosystem.
2. Fire and gravity may function as abiotic factors.
3. Parasites and symbionts are abiotic components.
4. Topography and wind are abiotic components.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Radiation, fire, gravity, topography and wind are abiotic factors. Parasites and symbionts are living, biotic components.
73.tq: Use the living-versus-non-living test to identify the incorrect statement.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which of the following correctly describes an ecosystem?
o: A biotic community and its non-living surroundings linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling
A group of abiotic factors independent of living organisms
A collection of animals without their physical surroundings
Only the plant community present in a geographical region
73.x: An ecosystem includes a biotic community and its non-living environment, connected through energy flow and nutrient cycling.
73.tq: Select the option containing both the living community and its physical environment.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: In an ecosystem, which of the following correctly describes the relationship between energy and nutrients?
o: Energy flows in one direction, whereas nutrients cycle through the ecosystem.
Energy cycles but nutrients flow only towards decomposers.
Both energy and nutrients cycle repeatedly in the same manner.
Neither energy nor nutrients move between trophic levels.
73.x: Energy moves unidirectionally through trophic levels, while nutrients are recycled through biogeochemical cycles.
73.tq: Distinguish the one-way movement of energy from the cyclical movement of nutrients.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which organisms primarily break down dead matter into inorganic nutrients?
73.x: Bacteria and fungi act as decomposers and convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients that can be reused by producers.
73.tq: Match the process of nutrient release with the organisms that perform decomposition.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Earthworms differ from decomposer bacteria and fungi chiefly because earthworms:
o: Fragment dead organic matter as detritivores
Occupy the producer level in every food chain
73.x: Earthworms are detritivores that fragment dead organic matter. Bacteria and fungi chemically decompose it into inorganic nutrients.
73.tq: Discriminate between physical fragmentation by detritivores and chemical decomposition by microbes.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Decomposers are regarded as a link between the biotic and abiotic components because they:
o: Convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients reused by producers
Prevent nutrient cycling in the soil
73.x: Decomposers release inorganic nutrients from dead organic matter, making them available again to producers and linking living and non-living components.
73.tq: Apply the link concept by tracing nutrients from dead organisms back to producers.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
73.x: Lions are tertiary consumers when they feed on other carnivores such as wolves. They are not primary consumers, which feed directly on producers.
73.tq: Check each organism against its usual feeding position and identify the reversed consumer level.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism or group)
 a. Humans
 b. Saprotrophs
 c. Reptiles
 d. Camel

List-II (Characteristic)
 i. Cold-blooded
 ii. Desert-adapted
 iii. Feed on dead matter
 iv. Omnivores

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Humans are omnivores, saprotrophs feed on dead matter, reptiles are cold-blooded, and camels are adapted to desert conditions.
73.tq: Begin with the distinctive camel and saprotroph pairs, then complete the remaining matches.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes macroconsumers from microconsumers?
o: Macroconsumers are phagotrophs, whereas microconsumers are saprotrophs.
Macroconsumers are abiotic, whereas microconsumers are biotic.
Macroconsumers manufacture inorganic nutrients, whereas microconsumers consume sunlight.
Macroconsumers are decomposers, whereas microconsumers are herbivores.
73.x: Macroconsumers, or phagotrophs, ingest food particles or organisms. Microconsumers, or saprotrophs, obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter.
73.tq: Use the feeding mode—ingestion versus saprotrophic absorption—to distinguish the two groups.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which of the following statements about natural and artificial ecosystems is correct?
o: Artificial ecosystems develop without appreciable human influence.
Natural ecosystems are created and maintained exclusively by humans.
Natural ecosystems develop with little human influence, whereas artificial ecosystems are man-made.
Artificial ecosystems cannot contain producers or decomposers.
73.x: Natural ecosystems develop with little human influence. Artificial ecosystems, such as crop fields and urban parks, are created or substantially managed by humans.
73.tq: Compare the ecosystems by their degree of human creation and management.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: A crop field and an urban park are best classified as:
73.x: Crop fields and urban parks are examples of artificial ecosystems because they are created or maintained through human intervention.
73.tq: Apply the natural-versus-man-made distinction to familiar examples.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: In a pond ecosystem, which of the following combinations is correctly arranged?
73.x: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are consumers, and bacteria and fungi act as decomposers in a pond ecosystem.
73.tq: Assign each pond organism according to its trophic or decomposer function.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following represents a grassland food chain mentioned in ecological examples?
o: Grass → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk
73.x: A grassland chain begins with grass, followed by herbivores such as grasshoppers or rabbits, and then predators such as snakes or hawks.
73.tq: Read the chain from producer to herbivore and then to predator.
73.sec: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following best describes the habitat of an organism?
o: The physical place where the organism lives
The total number of organisms in a population
The functional role performed by the organism in an ecosystem
The climatic region containing similar vegetation
73.x: Habitat is the physical place where an organism lives. Its functional role is described by the term niche.
73.tq: Use the habitat–niche distinction and identify the physical-location meaning.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: The term ‘niche’ refers to which one of the following?
o: The total population of different species in an area
The transition zone between two ecosystems
The functional role of an organism, including the food, space, time and conditions it uses
The physical area occupied by an organism
73.x: A niche is the functional role of an organism and includes the food, space, time and environmental conditions it uses.
73.tq: Discriminate between the physical place, habitat, and the functional role, niche.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: Natality in a population is concerned with
o: the number of individuals dying in a population
the number of births in a population
the proportion of males and females in a population
the distribution of individuals among age groups
73.x: Natality means births in a population. Its rate may be expressed as the number of individuals produced per female per unit time.
73.tq: Match the population attribute with the process it measures.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: Which of the following is NOT a population attribute?
73.x: Density, mortality, age structure and sex ratio are population attributes. Dominant vegetation is associated with the description of a biome.
73.tq: Find the item belonging to the neighbouring ecological level rather than the population level.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: A community in ecology consists of
o: all abiotic factors in a habitat
all individuals of one species in an area
all populations of different species in an area
73.x: A community comprises all populations of different species living in an area.
73.tq: Separate a community from a single-species population by checking the word ‘different’.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: A biome is primarily defined by its
o: number of species at an ecosystem boundary
73.x: A biome is a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation, such as rainforest, tundra or desert.
73.tq: Identify the defining pair in a classification question: climate plus dominant vegetation.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems.
2. Ecotones may show greater species richness because of the edge effect.
3. Mangroves and estuaries can exemplify ecotones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. An ecotone is a transition zone, and its boundary conditions may produce an edge effect and increased species richness.
73.tq: Check whether all statements describe the definition, examples and characteristic effect of an ecotone.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: The ability of an ecosystem to withstand a disturbance is known as
73.x: Resistance is the ability to withstand disturbance. Resilience is the ability to recover after disturbance.
73.tq: Separate the two similar terms by asking whether the ecosystem withstands or recovers from disturbance.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: The ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance is called
73.x: Resilience refers to the ability to recover after a disturbance, whereas resistance refers to withstanding it.
73.tq: Test the recovery meaning of resilience against the withstand meaning of resistance.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: Which one of the following combinations is most consistent with greater ecological stability?
o: Lower diversity and a simpler food web
A single producer and a single consumer
Higher diversity and greater food-web complexity
73.x: Ecological stability generally rises with increasing diversity and greater food-web complexity.
73.tq: Apply the relationship between diversity, web complexity and ecosystem stability.
73.sec: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

73.s: Which of the following statements regarding ecological pyramids is correct?
o: The base represents top consumers and the apex represents producers.
The base generally represents producers and the apex represents top consumers.
Ecological pyramids have only two types.
All organisms occupy only one trophic level.
73.x: The base of an ecological pyramid represents producers and the apex represents top consumers. The three types are pyramids of number, biomass and energy.
73.tq: Use the structural rule of ecological pyramids: producers at the base and top consumers at the apex.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: How many major types of ecological pyramids are recognised in the classification given below?
73.x: The three major types are the pyramid of number, the pyramid of biomass and the pyramid of energy.
73.tq: Count the named categories rather than confusing ecological pyramids with trophic levels.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: A pyramid of numbers is likely to be inverted in
o: a tree ecosystem with one tree supporting many insects
a simple grazing chain beginning with grasses
a crop field with many plants
73.x: A tree ecosystem may have one producer tree supporting numerous herbivorous insects, producing an inverted pyramid of numbers.
73.tq: Visualise the number of organisms at each level instead of their size or biomass.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: An inverted pyramid of numbers may also occur in
o: a forest floor litter chain only
73.x: Parasitic food chains can have fewer hosts supporting numerous parasites, resulting in an inverted pyramid of numbers.
73.tq: Recognise the host–parasite pattern as a standard exception to an upright number pyramid.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: In which one of the following ecosystems is an inverted pyramid of biomass characteristically observed?
73.x: In aquatic ecosystems, the small standing biomass of rapidly multiplying phytoplankton can support a larger biomass of zooplankton and fish.
73.tq: Compare standing biomass in terrestrial systems with rapidly turning-over phytoplankton in aquatic systems.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: Why can the biomass pyramid in an aquatic ecosystem be inverted?
o: Fish do not consume zooplankton in aquatic ecosystems.
Energy increases at every aquatic trophic level.
Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but rapidly support larger zooplankton and fish biomass.
73.x: Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but reproduce and are consumed rapidly, allowing them to support a larger standing biomass of zooplankton and fish.
73.tq: Distinguish standing biomass from productivity and identify the fast-turnover producer explanation.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: Which ecological pyramid can NEVER be inverted?
73.x: The energy pyramid is always upright because energy is lost as heat at every trophic transfer and cannot increase at higher levels.
73.tq: Look for the absolute exception and connect it with energy loss at each trophic transfer.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Energy is lost as heat at every trophic transfer.
2. Therefore, the energy pyramid is always upright.
3. A single species may occupy more than one trophic level in a food web.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. Heat loss keeps the energy pyramid upright, while omnivory may allow one species to occupy more than one trophic level.
73.tq: Link the physical rule of energy loss with the food-web exception concerning trophic levels.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Pyramid)
a. Number
b. Biomass
c. Energy
List-II (Characteristic)
i. Always upright
 ii. May be inverted in aquatic ecosystems
 iii. May be inverted in a tree ecosystem

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
73.x: The pyramid of number may be inverted in a tree ecosystem, the biomass pyramid may be inverted in aquatic systems, and the energy pyramid is always upright.
73.tq: Start from the sure pair that energy is always upright, then match the two inversion cases.
73.sec: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

73.s: Which of the following correctly represents producers in a terrestrial ecosystem?
o: Sulphur bacteria at deep-sea vents only
73.x: Herbs, shrubs and trees are the principal producers in terrestrial ecosystems.
73.tq: Match the producer group with its ecosystem rather than with an aquatic or vent environment.
73.sec: Producers in different ecosystems - terrestrial, aquatic, chemosynthetic

73.s: In an aquatic ecosystem, the producer group includes
o: phytoplankton, algae, and submerged and floating plants
73.x: Aquatic producers include phytoplankton, algae, and submerged and floating plants.
73.tq: Identify organisms capable of primary production in water and exclude aquatic consumers.
73.sec: Producers in different ecosystems - terrestrial, aquatic, chemosynthetic

73.s: The primary producers at deep-sea vents are chiefly
73.x: Chemosynthetic bacteria, including sulphur bacteria, use chemical energy rather than light at deep-sea vents.
73.tq: Apply the light-versus-chemical-energy distinction to a lightless ecosystem.
73.sec: Producers in different ecosystems - terrestrial, aquatic, chemosynthetic

73.s: A species whose effect on a community is far greater than would be expected from its abundance is called a
73.x: A keystone species has an ecological effect far larger than its abundance; its removal may cause the community to collapse.
73.tq: Use the defining phrase ‘effect far larger than abundance’ to identify a keystone species.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: The sea star Pisaster ochraceus is regarded as a keystone species because it
73.x: Pisaster ochraceus is a keystone sea star that controls mussels in intertidal zones. This example is associated with the work of Robert Paine.
73.tq: Use the species–ecological effect association rather than the general definition alone.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: Which one of the following is a foundation species?
73.x: Foundation species create or shape the habitat itself; corals and kelp are examples.
73.tq: Distinguish habitat-building species from charismatic and environmental-indicator species.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: A species selected to draw public support for conservation because of its charismatic appeal is known as a
73.x: A flagship species is a charismatic species used to draw public support for conservation; the tiger and giant panda are examples.
73.tq: Identify the public-support function rather than an ecosystem-function role.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: Lichens are commonly used as indicators of
73.x: Lichens can indicate environmental health and are particularly used as indicators of sulphur dioxide pollution.
73.tq: Match the indicator organism with the environmental condition it signals.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: The umbrella species concept implies that protection of a wide-ranging species
o: always increases the number of producers
protects many other species sharing its habitat
73.x: Protecting a wide-ranging umbrella species can protect many other species that share its habitat and range.
73.tq: Apply the spatial-cover meaning of an umbrella species to a conservation situation.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: Which pair is NOT correctly matched?
o: Keystone species — effect much larger than its abundance
Umbrella species — attracts public support mainly through charisma
Foundation species — creates or shapes habitat
73.x: Attracting public support through charisma is the role of a flagship species. An umbrella species is wide-ranging, and its protection benefits many other species.
73.tq: Find the swapped definition among closely related conservation roles.
73.sec: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

73.s: Which adaptation is characteristic of halophytes growing in saline soils or mangroves?
o: Reduced roots and floating leaves only
Absence of any specialised root system
73.x: Halophytes may possess pneumatophores for breathing, salt glands and vivipary; mangrove plants such as Rhizophora are examples.
73.tq: Match the habitat type with its distinctive structural adaptations.
73.sec: Habitat adaptations - halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

73.s: Which of the following is correctly associated with xerophytes?
o: Thin cuticle and reduced roots for floating
Thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines, succulence and CAM
73.x: Xerophytes are adapted to deserts through features such as thick cuticles, sunken stomata, spines, succulence and CAM; Opuntia is an example.
73.tq: Recognise the water-conservation package typical of desert plants.
73.sec: Habitat adaptations - halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

73.s: Aerenchyma, reduced roots, thin cuticle and floating leaves are characteristic adaptations of
73.x: Hydrophytes are water plants and commonly possess aerenchyma, reduced roots, thin cuticles and floating leaves. Hydrilla and lotus are examples.
73.tq: Match the structural features with the water-adapted plant group.
73.sec: Habitat adaptations - halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

73.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Rhizophora — halophyte
2. Opuntia — xerophyte
3. Hydrilla — hydrophyte
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
73.x: All three pairs are correct. Rhizophora is a salt-tolerant mangrove plant, Opuntia is a desert plant, and Hydrilla is an aquatic plant.
73.tq: Verify each organism against its habitat adaptation before selecting the coded combination.
73.sec: Habitat adaptations - halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

73.s: Which one of the following pairs correctly represents mutualism?
o: Lichen consisting of alga and fungus
73.x: Mutualism is an interaction in which both partners benefit. Lichen represents the association of an alga and a fungus, with a positive effect on both.
73.tq: Identify the interaction from the sign and a standard example.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Commensalism — Orchid growing as an epiphyte on mango
2. Parasitism — Cuscuta on a host plant
3. Amensalism — Penicillium inhibiting bacteria
4. Competition — Tiger and deer
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
73.x: Orchid on mango is commensalism, Cuscuta is parasitism and Penicillium inhibiting bacteria is amensalism. Tiger and deer illustrate predation, not competition.
73.tq: Find the swapped example by distinguishing predation from competition.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: In which interaction are both species adversely affected because they use the same limited resource?
73.x: Competition has a -/- effect because both species are adversely affected while using the same limited resource.
73.tq: Use the sign convention to identify the interaction.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
73.x: Neutralism denotes an interaction in which neither species is significantly affected, represented by 0/0. Amensalism is -/0, predation is +/- and commensalism is +/0.
73.tq: Discriminate closely related interaction signs.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: The association between a fig tree and a fig wasp is an example of
73.x: The fig wasp pollinates the fig and obtains a breeding site, making the association a coevolved mutualistic relationship.
73.tq: Apply the benefit-benefit relationship to a specialised natural association.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: Which of the following pairs is associated with sexual deceit during pollination?
73.x: The Ophrys orchid attracts bees through sexual deceit, thereby facilitating pollination.
73.tq: Test a distinctive feature of a coevolved pair.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s:
With reference to ecological interactions, consider the following statements:
1. Intraspecific interactions occur among members of the same species.
2. Interspecific interactions occur among members of different species.
3. Interspecific interactions can be beneficial, harmful or neutral.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Intraspecific interactions occur within a species. Interspecific interactions occur between different species and may have positive, negative or neutral effects.
73.tq: Build the answer by separating same-species and different-species relationships.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: Competing species may coexist when they
o: avoid all interaction with other species
use different parts or forms of a shared resource
73.x: Resource partitioning permits competing species to coexist by using different portions of a resource, such as different parts of the same plant.
73.tq: Apply the ecological principle of resource partitioning.
73.sec: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs  [APPSC]

73.s: Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes habitat from niche?
o: Habitat and niche are identical terms.
Habitat is the physical place, whereas niche is the functional role of a species.
Habitat is the functional role, whereas niche is the physical place.
A niche can be occupied by unlimited species with identical roles.
73.x: Habitat is the physical place or address of an organism. Niche is its functional role or profession in that habitat.
73.tq: Separate the address concept from the profession concept.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. One habitat may contain many species.
2. All habitats are environments.
3. All environments are habitats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: A habitat is a particular physical place within the broader concept of environment. Thus, one habitat can contain many species and all habitats are environments, but all environments are not habitats.
73.tq: Spot the reversed universal statement in a definition-based question.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: The fundamental niche of a species refers to
o: the actual range occupied after competition
the full range of conditions and resources it could use in the absence of other species
73.x: Fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources available to a species when competition and other biological limitations are absent.
73.tq: Distinguish potential range from actual range.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following best describes a realised niche?
o: The physical address of a species
The complete potential niche without competitors
The actual range used after competition and other limitations
The geographical range of an entire biome
73.x: A realised niche is the portion of the fundamental niche actually used under competition and other ecological constraints.
73.tq: Use the word actual to identify the realised niche.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
73.x: Grinnell proposed the habitat niche concept in 1917. Elton is associated with the functional niche, while Hutchinson proposed the n-dimensional niche.
73.tq: Match proponents with the specific form of niche concept.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: The n-dimensional niche concept was proposed by
73.x: G. E. Hutchinson proposed the n-dimensional niche concept in 1957.
73.tq: Link the distinctive terminology with its proponent and year.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: A koala, which feeds mainly on eucalyptus, is best described as a
73.x: A specialist uses a narrow range of resources. Dependence of the koala mainly on eucalyptus is an example of narrow niche breadth.
73.tq: Infer niche breadth from the range of resources used.
73.sec: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: An ecotone is best described as
o: the centre of a climax community
a region having no species interaction
a uniform stand of a single forest type
a transition zone where two communities or biomes meet and integrate
73.x: An ecotone is a transition zone between two biological communities or biomes, generally having intermediate conditions.
73.tq: Identify the transition-zone definition without confusing it with a single community.
73.sec: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Uniform forest stand — ecotone between two communities
Estuary — fresh water and salt water interface
73.x: A uniform stand of one forest type is a single community, not an ecotone. Mangroves, estuaries and riverbanks represent the stated transition zones.
73.tq: Find the exception by rejecting a single-community area.
73.sec: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which of the following correctly represents the habitat transition associated with a grassland ecotone?
73.x: Grassland is identified as an ecotonal region between forest and desert conditions.
73.tq: Discriminate among ecotone pairs by matching the habitat combination.
73.sec: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: The edge effect refers to the phenomenon in which an ecotone generally has
o: fewer species than either adjoining community
only species from the larger adjoining community
more species and higher density of some species than either adjoining community
73.x: The edge effect is the increased number of species and increased density of some species in an ecotone. Such organisms are called edge species.
73.tq: Use the comparison with adjoining communities to identify the edge effect.
73.sec: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: A higher concentration of birds at the boundary between a forest and a desert is an example of
73.x: The increased bird density at a forest-desert boundary illustrates the edge effect and the occurrence of edge species.
73.tq: Apply the edge-effect definition to a habitat-boundary situation.
73.sec: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Mortality — births per female per unit time
Carrying capacity — number of predators only
73.x: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area. Mortality refers to deaths per unit time, while natality refers to births.
73.tq: Separate the basic population attributes by their measured quantities.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: An age pyramid with a broad base and triangular shape indicates a population that is
73.x: A triangular age pyramid has a large proportion of pre-reproductive individuals and indicates an expanding population.
73.tq: Read population trend from the shape of the age pyramid.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched?
73.x: A triangular age pyramid indicates an expanding population. Bell-shaped and urn-shaped pyramids indicate stable and declining populations respectively.
73.tq: Compare the three age-pyramid forms with their population trends.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: A population showing a J-shaped growth curve is characterised by
73.x: The J-curve represents exponential growth, expressed as dN/dt = rN, when resources are assumed to be unlimited.
73.tq: Associate the curve shape with the growth equation and resource condition.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: The S-shaped growth curve of a population is associated with
o: logistic growth approaching carrying capacity K
73.x: The S-curve represents logistic growth, in which population growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity K; it is expressed as dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K.
73.tq: Distinguish logistic growth from exponential growth by the role of K.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which of the following is characteristic of an r-selected species?
o: Stable population in a saturated habitat only
Few large offspring and extensive parental care
Long life and population size close to K
Many small offspring and little parental care
73.x: r-selected species generally produce many small offspring, provide little parental care and often inhabit unstable environments.
73.tq: Contrast r-selected traits with the K-selected strategy.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding r-selected and K-selected species:
1. Insects and weeds commonly show r-selected characteristics.
2. Elephants and humans commonly show K-selected characteristics.
3. K-selected species generally produce few large offspring and provide considerable parental care.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. r-selected species include many insects and weeds, whereas elephants and humans illustrate the K-selected strategy of fewer offspring and greater care.
73.tq: Combine examples with the contrasting reproductive strategies.
73.sec: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Who wrote the book *Animal Ecology* and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers?
73.x: Charles Elton wrote *Animal Ecology* in 1927 and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers.
73.tq: Match the publication and contribution with the ecologist.
73.sec: Ecologists → contribution  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: *Fundamentals of Ecology* was written by
73.x: Eugene P. Odum wrote *Fundamentals of Ecology* in 1953 and is regarded as the father of modern ecosystem ecology.
73.tq: Use the book-title trap to distinguish closely associated ecologists.
73.sec: Ecologists → contribution  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Henry C. Cowles — ecological succession in Lake Michigan dunes
G. E. Hutchinson — father of Indian ecology
73.x: Henry C. Cowles studied ecological succession in the dunes of Lake Michigan. Hutchinson is associated with the n-dimensional niche, Ramdeo Misra with Indian ecology and Odum with ecosystem ecology.
73.tq: Match each ecologist with the distinctive contribution rather than the general subject.
73.sec: Ecologists → contribution  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Ramdeo Misra is popularly known as the
73.x: Ramdeo Misra is recognised as the father of Indian ecology.
73.tq: Test a national attribution against similarly worded ecological titles.
73.sec: Ecologists → contribution  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Rule — Ecogeographic trait
o: Bergmann — Number of vertebrae in fish
Allen — Body colouration in warm-humid climates
Jordan — Number of vertebrae in fish
Gloger — Sexual size dimorphism in shorebirds
73.x: Jordan's rule relates temperature to the number of vertebrae in fish; colder conditions are associated with a greater number of vertebrae. Bergmann concerns body size, Allen concerns appendages, and Gloger concerns colouration.
73.tq: Use direct rule-trait discrimination and reject the swapped associations.
73.sec: Ecogeographic rules → trait  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ecogeographic rules:
1. Bergmann's rule relates colder climates with larger body size.
2. Allen's rule relates colder climates with shorter ears and limbs.
3. Rensch's rule concerns size dimorphism between sexes and has been tested on shorebirds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. Bergmann, Allen and Rensch respectively describe body size, appendage length and sexual size dimorphism.
73.tq: Test each rule independently before selecting the coded combination.
73.sec: Ecogeographic rules → trait  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Gloger’s rule primarily explains variation in which of the following characteristics in relation to climate?
73.x: Gloger’s rule relates climate to colouration; warm and humid environments are generally associated with darker colouration.
73.tq: Direct one-fact recall of a confusable rule-trait relationship.
73.sec: Ecogeographic rules → trait  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following represents the correct ecological order from the smallest to the largest level?
o: Organism → community → population → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Population → organism → community → biome → ecosystem → biosphere
Organism → ecosystem → population → community → biome → biosphere
73.x: The ecological order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
73.tq: Check the hierarchy sequentially from the individual level upward.
73.sec: Levels of ecological organisation - organism to biosphere  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Which of the following gives the complete hierarchy of ecological organisation in the correct order?

1. Atoms
2. Molecules
3. Protoplasm
4. Cells
5. Tissues
6. Organs
7. Organisms
8. Populations
9. Communities
10. Ecosystems
11. Biomes
12. Biosphere
73.x: The complete sequence proceeds from atoms to molecules, protoplasm, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes and biosphere.
73.tq: Arrange the levels by moving from molecular organisation to global ecological organisation.
73.sec: Levels of ecological organisation - organism to biosphere  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Consider the following statements about the biosphere:
1. It is absent at the poles, the highest peaks and the deepest oceans.
2. Fungal and bacterial spores occurring above 8,000 metres are dormant.
3. Energy enters the biosphere from the Sun, while nutrients are recycled within it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements correctly describe the limits and functioning of the biosphere. Solar energy enters the system, whereas nutrients undergo internal recycling.
73.tq: Combine three independent factual statements and identify the inclusive option.
73.sec: Levels of ecological organisation - organism to biosphere  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s: A biome is best described as which one of the following?
o: A transition zone between two adjacent ecosystems
An artificial ecosystem maintained only by human beings
A small community containing only one species
A large natural community of flora and fauna over a major habitat, shaped mainly by climate
73.x: A biome is a large natural community of flora and fauna occupying a major habitat and shaped by climate. It contains many habitats.
73.tq: Distinguish the definition of a biome from community, ecosystem and ecotone.
73.sec: Biomes of the world → climate + vegetation, anthropogenic biomes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Biome)
(a) Tundra
(b) Taiga
(c) Savanna
(d) Desert

List-II (Characteristic vegetation)
(i) Xerophytes
(ii) Evergreen conifers
(iii) Mosses, lichens and shrubs such as bearberry
(iv) Grasses with scattered trees

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Tundra supports mosses, lichens and bearberry; taiga has evergreen conifers; savanna has grasses with scattered trees; deserts support xerophytes.
73.tq: Start with the sure biome-vegetation pairs and eliminate codes containing reversals.
73.sec: Biomes of the world → climate + vegetation, anthropogenic biomes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Tundra — Very cold climate and permafrost
Taiga — Long cold winters and distribution only in the Northern Hemisphere
Tropical rainforest — Very low rainfall and xerophytic vegetation
73.x: Tropical rainforests have a hot and wet climate throughout the year and dense, multilayered evergreen vegetation. Very low rainfall and xerophytes characterise deserts.
73.tq: Find the one biome-climate pair that belongs to a different biome.
73.sec: Biomes of the world → climate + vegetation, anthropogenic biomes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s: The vegetation of a tropical rainforest is generally characterised by which of the following?
o: Sparse grasses and scattered thorn trees
Dense, multi-layered evergreen vegetation with very high diversity
Mosses and lichens above the tree line
Only deciduous trees adapted to prolonged drought
73.x: Tropical rainforests are hot and wet throughout the year and possess dense, multi-layered evergreen vegetation with the richest diversity.
73.tq: Use the climate-vegetation association to identify the biome.
73.sec: Biomes of the world → climate + vegetation, anthropogenic biomes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s: Anthropogenic biomes, also called anthromes, are ecological units shaped by which of the following?
o: Sustained human use such as croplands, villages and cities
73.x: Anthropogenic biomes are ecological units shaped by sustained human use and include croplands, villages and cities.
73.tq: Apply the definition to examples of human-shaped ecological units.
73.sec: Biomes of the world → climate + vegetation, anthropogenic biomes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

73.s: Arthur Tansley defined an ecosystem in 1935 as a system resulting from the integration of which of the following?
o: Only the physical and chemical components of an area
All food chains present in a biome
Only the living organisms of a habitat
All living and non-living factors of the environment
73.x: In 1935, Arthur Tansley described an ecosystem as a system resulting from the integration of all living and non-living factors of the environment.
73.tq: Test the precise wording of a definition along with its associated year and scientist.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Which of the following is included in the structural aspect of an ecosystem?

1. Biotic community
2. Abiotic materials
3. Species composition
4. Trophic levels

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Ecosystem structure includes the biotic community, abiotic materials, species composition and trophic levels. Energy flow and nutrient cycling are functional aspects.
73.tq: Separate structural components from ecosystem processes before choosing the code.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following represents a functional process of an ecosystem rather than its structure?
73.x: Nutrient cycling is an ecosystem function. Species composition, trophic levels and abiotic materials are elements of ecosystem structure.
73.tq: Discriminate between the structure and function columns of an ecosystem.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Energy flow in an ecosystem is one-way and begins primarily with the Sun.
2. Nutrient cycling takes place through biogeochemical cycles.
3. Self-regulation is one of the functions of an ecosystem.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Energy flow, nutrient cycling and self-regulation are all functional characteristics of ecosystems. Energy moves one-way, whereas nutrients are cycled.
73.tq: Test several functions together while distinguishing energy flow from nutrient cycling.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the exchange characteristics of ecosystems and the Earth?
o: Ecosystems are open for energy and matter, while the Earth is open for energy but nearly closed for matter
Ecosystems are open only for matter, while the Earth is closed for energy
Ecosystems are closed for both energy and matter, while the Earth is open for both
Both ecosystems and the Earth are completely closed systems
73.x: Ecosystems exchange both energy and matter with their surroundings. The Earth receives energy from outside but is nearly closed with respect to matter.
73.tq: Compare open and closed characteristics across ecosystems and the Earth.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: The flow of energy through an ecosystem is governed by which broad principle?
73.x: Energy flow in ecosystems obeys the laws of thermodynamics. Energy is transferred between trophic levels with substantial loss as heat.
73.tq: Directly identify the governing scientific principle from the process described.
73.sec: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: An abiotic factor is best defined as which one of the following?
o: An organism that obtains food from dead organic matter
Any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment
A living component occupying the highest trophic level
A biological interaction between two species
73.x: An abiotic factor is any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment, such as light, temperature, water or soil.
73.tq: Use the precise definition rather than examples alone.
73.sec: Abiotic factors - climatic, edaphic, topographic; limiting-factor laws  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of abiotic factor)
(a) Climatic
(b) Edaphic
(c) Topographic

List-II (Examples)
(i) Altitude, slope and aspect
(ii) Light, temperature and rainfall
(iii) Soil texture, pH and minerals

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Climatic factors include light, temperature and rainfall; edaphic factors relate to soil; topographic factors include altitude, slope and aspect.
73.tq: Start from the meaning of edaphic and topographic before matching the remaining pair.
73.sec: Abiotic factors - climatic, edaphic, topographic; limiting-factor laws  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which one of the following is NOT included in the listed abiotic components of an ecosystem?
73.x: Species composition is a structural biotic feature of an ecosystem, not an abiotic component. Energy, radiation, temperature, water, gases, wind, fire, gravity, topography, substratum and soil are abiotic components.
73.tq: Find the biological term embedded among physical and chemical factors.
73.sec: Abiotic factors - climatic, edaphic, topographic; limiting-factor laws  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Liebig’s Law of the Minimum states that the growth of an organism is limited by which of the following?
o: The factor that changes most rapidly
The factor present in greatest quantity
The average value of all environmental factors
73.x: Liebig’s Law of the Minimum states that growth is limited by the nutrient or factor in shortest supply.
73.tq: Distinguish the minimum-law principle from the broader law of tolerance.
73.sec: Abiotic factors - climatic, edaphic, topographic; limiting-factor laws  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

73.s: Which statement correctly expresses Shelford’s Law of Tolerance?
o: An organism is unaffected by excessive quantities of environmental factors
Only deficiency of a factor can limit an organism
Growth depends exclusively on the nutrient in shortest supply
Both too little and too much of an environmental factor can limit an organism
73.x: Shelford’s Law of Tolerance holds that both insufficient and excessive levels of an environmental factor can limit an organism.
